newsitem.title: MEXICO: Family of fallen Mexican general defends him.
newsitem.headline: Family of fallen Mexican general defends him.

text.p: The wife and daughter of Mexico's disgraced former anti-drugs chief defended him on Thursday against charges of narcotics corruption, alleging he was being framed by high government and army officials.
In an interview with Reuters and the CBS Telenoticias Spanish language television network, Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo's wife and daughter said they were convinced of his innocence.

General Gutierrez Rebollo was fired as chief of Mexico's National Institute for Drug Combat (INCD) and arrested in February on charges of taking protection money from Amado Carrillo Fuentes, leader of the Juarez drug cartel.
Daughter Teresa de Jesus Gutierrez Ramirez said there was hard evidence proving his innocence but she could not reveal details yet "because that would expose the defence lawyer."

A Defence Ministry spokesman told Reuters officials there could not respond to the charges on Thursday. A spokesman for President Ernesto Zedillo said his office would leave any comment to the Defence Ministry.

The bombshell of the general's arrest rocked Mexico in the highly publicised run-up to the U.S. process of determining which countries to certify as aid-worthy allies in the fight against drugs. It was also a blow to the Clinton administration, which weeks earlier had publicly praised Gutierrez Rebollo as an honest public servant.

Gutierrez Rebollo's wife, Maria Teresa Ramirez de Gutierrez, dismissed the government's allegations that the general enjoyed a secret luxury lifestyle. "My husband was a straight man, strong, firm in his work. We lived a simple life. You can't hide money," she said.

His daughter linked her father's arrest to a dispute he had with his superior, Defence Minister Gen. Enrique Cervantes Aguirre. She said that in a Feb. 6 meeting Cervantes cancelled a planned U.S.-aided operation organised by Gutierrez Rebollo to capture a leader of the Arellano Felix drug cartel, a rival organisation to that of Amado Carrillo.
"My father's response was to say that he wasn't put in his job to play the fool ... that he was there to clean up the (anti-drugs) institute," she said.
"My father said that there was a time limit (on the operation) because in a meeting in Washington it was mentioned where some of these people might be."

When Gutierrez Rebollo opposed the defence minister, his daughter said, he was arrested, taken to the military hospital, sedated and put under heavy guard. He also had a catheter inserted into his heart unnecessarily, she said.
Twelve days later, on Feb. 18, Cervantes announced that Gutierrez Rebollo had been arrested and charged with betraying his office. If convicted, he could face the death penalty.
Asked why the government might have wanted to frame her father, Gutierrez Ramirez said: "He knows things that go up the line, both in the military and political (structure)."
But she refused to amplify, saying she feared "reprisals."
"My father worked with the DEA (U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration)," she said. "Do you think it's easy to fool the DEA?"

But she did not dispute that her father had secretly rented an apartment for his mistress in Mexico City, as authorities have alleged. Mexican authorities say another apartment in the same building was used by Amado Carrillo, but the daughter called that a "coincidence."
The general's wife, asked if the impassioned defence of her husband was only a natural reaction, replied: "Truly, believe me, in the name of God, I am telling the truth."
